title: Ever virgin (CCC 499–501)
hook: Catholics and Orthodox hold that Mary remained a virgin; some Protestants read the brothers of Jesus differently

segments.voice: Yesterday, dogma: lights along the path, and four of them about Mary. Your line was four teachings. Could you name all four before dinner? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-eight.

Jesus comes back to his own hometown and teaches in the synagogue, and the town can't get past who he is. Isn't this the carpenter? Isn't his mother called Mary? And then they name names: his brothers, James and Joseph and Simon and Jude, and his sisters too, right here among us. Readers still stop at that line and ask: brothers? Today takes the second of yesterday's four teachings slowly, and that question with it. Today's word: ever virgin.
screen: `ISN'T THIS THE CARPENTER?` → `HIS BROTHERS, HIS SISTERS.` → `EVER VIRGIN.`

segments.voice: First, what the Church teaches. The Catechism says Mary's virginity was real and lasting: before Jesus' birth, in it, and for the rest of her life. In the liturgy she's called ever virgin. Second, where it starts. When the angel tells Mary she will bear a son, she asks, in Luke's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "How shall this be done, because I know not man?" The Church reads her whole life as a yes given entirely to God, and her virginity as a sign of that: a heart, and a body, kept for the one who came to live in it. Third, the brothers. The Catechism answers the Nazareth line directly. It notes that James and Joseph, two of the names, are called elsewhere in Matthew the sons of another Mary, a disciple of Jesus. And it says that the brothers and sisters are close relations of Jesus, in a way of speaking the Old Testament also uses, where relatives are called brothers. Some early Christian writers thought they were Joseph's children from before he married Mary. Others thought they were cousins. Fourth, who reads what. The Catholic and Orthodox churches both teach that Mary remained a virgin; the Orthodox call her ever-virgin in their prayers. Some Protestants read the brothers as later children of Mary and Joseph, and some do not. Each reads the same pages carefully. And one more line from the Catechism: Jesus is Mary's only son, but her motherhood reaches out to everyone he came to save. Ever virgin doesn't make her distant. In Catholic teaching, it frees her to be mother to many.
screen: `BEFORE, DURING, AND AFTER.` · `I KNOW NOT MAN.` · `THE BROTHERS: CLOSE RELATIONS.` · `ONLY SON, MOTHER OF MANY.` · then, large: `HOW SHALL THIS BE DONE?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for understanding. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one teaching, about Mary or anything else, that you find hard, or that people you love read differently. Don't argue it out. Just hold it, the way Mary held the angel's words and asked her honest question: how shall this be done? Let the question be a real one. If you pray, you can ask God for understanding, for yourself and for the people who see it another way. If you don't pray, simply rest with the question, open. The bell holds the time.
Ever virgin. Mary's lasting virginity, before, during and after Jesus' birth, as Catholics and Orthodox teach it: a life given entirely to God. Today's word.
Your line: ever virgin. Today, when you meet a view different from your own, ask one honest question about it before you answer. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Catholics call Mary ever virgin in the liturgy, including in the Confiteor at Mass, and the Orthodox call her ever-virgin in their prayers; the teaching is explained in the Catechism, paragraphs 496 to 501.

fork.setup: you're Mary. an angel says you'll bear a son. what do you say first?
options: an honest question: how shall this be done?
fork.reveal: she asks, how shall this be done, because I know not man? the Church reads her question and her yes as one whole gift to God.

original.note: Greek: ever-virgin, the title used of Mary in Orthodox prayers.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Gospels clearly say Jesus had younger siblings.
what it means: the Church reads the brothers and sisters as close relations, and holds that Mary remained a virgin.
what a scholar hears: CCC 500 pointing to Matthew 13:55 with 27:56, where James and Joseph are sons of another Mary, and to the Old Testament's wide use of brother.

notes: The index hook says 'many Protestants'; under the claims rule the script says 'some Protestants... and some do not'. Hook line reworded; the index hook is kept in meta.

Hook reworded from Mark 6:3 / Matthew 13:55 (unquoted). Matthew names Joses/Joseph, Simon and Jude; Mark names James, Joses, Jude and Simon. The script lists four names without saying which Gospel's order. Confirm.

CCC 499–501 paraphrased. CCC 500 cites Matthew 13:55, 28:1 and 27:56 and Genesis 13:8, 14:16, 29:15. The two early explanations (Joseph's earlier children; cousins) are not in the CCC and come from patristic tradition (e.g. the Protoevangelium of James; Jerome). Confirm they may stand without citation.
howItsDone mentions the Confiteor ('blessed Mary ever-Virgin'); confirm. Paragraph range 496–501 stated as a citation, not a claim.
Original ἀειπάρθενος; confirm accent and transliteration.

Editor pass: 'Catholics and Orthodox Christians both hold' changed to what the two churches teach (no claim about every believer); Mary's question in the practice and fork restored to the exact Douay wording, 'how shall this be done'.
